Design factors affecting microplastic retention, removal, and generation in structural best management practices

Project Number

PROJECT HIGHLIGHT

This project examined how rain gardens and other stormwater infrastructure designed to control runoff retain and release microplastics. Researchers studied 18 sites across Los Angeles and found that how these systems are designed, including whether they have plants, what type of soil mix they use and whether they have sediment traps, matters more for trapping microplastics than the income level or land use of the surrounding neighborhood. The findings show that design improvements can significantly boost the ability of stormwater systems to capture microplastics and reduce pollution in waterways.

 

PROJECT SUMMARY

Stormwater best management practices (BMPs) are systems like rain gardens and permeable pavements that help control rainwater runoff. Instead of letting rainwater rush quickly into streams and rivers, these green infrastructure systems mimic nature by encouraging water to soak into the ground.

This study examined 18 rain gardens and similar systems across Los Angeles County in neighborhoods with different income levels and land uses. Researchers collected soil samples at different depths and counted the microplastic particles to understand which factors influence where microplastics accumulate. They also ran laboratory experiments to test how different soil materials and conditions affect whether microplastics stay trapped or wash away.

The research revealed several important findings. First, microplastics are spread fairly evenly across Los Angeles regardless of neighborhood income or location, likely because wind and stormwater carry these particles widely across the urban landscape. Second, while these systems normally trap about 95% of incoming microplastics, laboratory results show that up to 40% of accumulated particles can be washed out during storms, significantly reducing effectiveness. Third, design choices make the biggest difference in performance: systems with more plants, deeper soil layers and finer soil textures (rather than just sand or compost alone) do a much better job keeping microplastics from moving deeper into the ground or washing away. These results provide practical guidance for improving how rain gardens and similar systems are built and maintained to better protect California's waterways and coastal areas from plastic pollution.

This project is funded by the California Ocean Protection Council (OPC) under Agreement No.C0223003, and is administered by California Sea Grant.
